newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU jobs woes to dominate Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: EU jobs woes to dominate Amsterdam summit.

text.p: Ask most European Union leaders what the biggest problem facing the 15-nation bloc is and chances are high they will say unemployment.

So going into Monday and Tuesday's EU summit in Amsterdam, the leaders were expected to make much of giving higher priority to the fight against mass unemployment, calling for a closer link between jobs and the planned single currency.
The need to bring down the Union's jobless rate of 10.9 percent has taken on an extra sense of urgency following the leftist shift in recent elections in both France and Britain.
Their arrival at the negotiating table virtually ensures that a revised EU treaty will for the first time include a special chapter on employment.

"There is no doubt that unemployment is higher on the agenda in all respects, both in the EMU and in the IGC context," one Nordic EU diplomat said, referring to the inter-governmental conference on a new treaty. "All this is somehow tied together."

While many remain sceptical that EU leaders can actually do much to help Europe's 18 million unemployed, recent events signal that the new French government is determined to live up to campaign pledges.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said he is concerned that a so-called stability pact, designed to keep budget deficits tight once monetary union is launched, does not do enough for employment.
British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, saying he and Strauss-Kahn were in "complete agreement" that jobs was the key issue for Europe, has also tabled a plan on job creation.

Even Germany, despite initial misgivings that it might interfere with EMU and raise unrealistic expectations among Europe's citizens, has come around to the idea as long as it does not create costly jobs schemes.
The employment title is expected to include a commitment to develop a "coordinated strategy for employment" within the bloc.
To do this, the EU would produce an annual report, adopt incentive measures, set up an Employment Committee and may even issue recommendations on employment policy to member states.
But there are still strong doubts about what contribution, if any, an employment chapter could make to help create jobs.

"We're only talking about declarations and commitments. We're not talking about anything that will itself hold the key to solving the employment problem," said Stanley Crossick, chairman of the European Policy Centre think-tank.
